artworks.title: Ming Smith: Jazz Requiem – Notations in Blue
artworks.description: In the Whittemore and Noonan Galleries. Photographs by Ming Smith from the 1970s to now, shaped by dance, music and her years travelling in Europe; many printed large. Smith embodies a tenet of the Black Arts Movement: “owning the images that we saw of ourselves.” Curated by Daisy Desrosiers (The Gund at Kenyon College).

artworks.title: Franne Davids and the World She Painted
artworks.description: The first museum show of Franne Davids (1950–2022), born in Waterbury: living with schizophrenia, she painted more than 400 pictures in her parents’ basement, mostly of women she called her “girls”, her imaginary friends. Organized by Chief Curator Rebecca McNamara.

artworks.title: The Waterbury Button Museum
artworks.description: More than 10,000 buttons from a collection of 20,000, made over 200 years in Waterbury, the “Brass City”, and around the world: carved cinnabar from Asia, Japanese netsuke, 1930s Bakelite, bouquets of human hair under glass, military buttons, Queen Victoria’s black glass, French “habitat” buttons with insects under glass, and four engraved buttons from George Washington’s coat. Assembled by Warren F. Kaynor for the Waterbury Button Company, given in 1999.

artworks.title: Bessie Smith Close Up
artworks.description:
About Face: 250 Years of American Portraits
April 26, 2026 – August 16, 2026
Born into poverty in Chattanooga, Tennessee, Bessie Smith (1894–1937) defied the circumstances of her upbringing to become the most celebrated blues artist of her time. Known as the “Empress of the Blues,” she began her career traveling through the South singing in tent shows, bars, and theaters before making her way to Philadelphia, which she would eventually call home.
By the early 1920s, Smith recorded more than 160 songs for Columbia Records, becoming the first blues singer to reach mass audiences and the highest-paid Black entertainer of her time. Her lyrics were powerful narratives of the African American experience, focusing on social and economic struggles, racial injustice, gender inequality, and the complexities of love. Stella Bloch painted Smith during this career high, capturing her prideful posture as she projected her voice to fill large theaters.
Smith’s life was cut short in 1937 at age 43 following a car accident near Clarksdale, Mississippi, where racial segregation at Southern hospitals delayed necessary medical care, and her injuries became fatal. Despite this tragedy, her legacy endures. With her barrier-breaking career, Smith forged a path for generations of Black artists to follow. She was posthumously inducted into the inaugural class of the Blues Hall of Fame (1980) and into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame (1989).
Staff Favorites from the Mattatuck Collection
January 18, 2026 – April 12, 2026
“I love Bessie Smith. I remember going to see her with my mother and grandmother in the city. She was such an exceptional jazz singer. She would always be wearing a beautiful rose in her hair. Her expression comes off as very sad to me in this work.” - Staff Member: Barbara
Hepburn, Visitor Services
The Art of Leisure
April 12, 2025 – June 15, 2025
Bessie Smith, known as the “Empress of Blues,” received acclaim for her powerful and emotive voice as well as her captivating stage presence. Artist and dancer Stella Bloch, a longtime admirer of Smith, captures the famed singer in a reverent moment of song. Bloch’s expressive brush strokes seem melodic themselves, alternating between short and long beats on the paper.

In the Mattatuck’s collection: it may be in storage today, ask whether it is on view.

artworks.title: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
artworks.description:
About Face: 250 Years of American Portraits
April 26, 2026 – August 16, 2026
Charlotte Perkins Gilman (1860–1935), born in Hartford, was a feminist, writer, and advocate for social reform, promoting the professionalization of domestic responsibilities and childcare, among other strategies toward gender equality and economic independence for women. Her 1892 short story “The Yellow Wall-Paper” describes one woman’s experience with a “rest cure” for “temporary nervous depression” (likely what we understand today to be postpartum depression). In the story, the protagonist’s physician-husband forces her to remain in a summer home with no intellectual stimulation; she descends into madness, a clear statement on the negative psychological and emotional impact of restricting women’s ambitions outside the domestic space.
Depicted here by contemporary artist Suzanne Benton, Gilman remains an inspiring writer and thinker to many feminists, writers, sociologists, and scholars today.

In the Mattatuck’s collection: it may be in storage today, ask whether it is on view.
